title: Compression at the Edge — NVIDIA, Unsloth, HuggingFace, Ollama

primary.label: Inference & Model Systems
primary.rationale: The entire panel is about model compression and quantization. NVFP4 (4-bit float with microscaling), post-training quantization, quantization-aware distillation, KV cache compression, dynamic activation sparsity, and serving quantized models are the dominant subjects. The taxonomy inclusion criteria explicitly lists 'Quantization, speculative decoding, or KV-cache engineering as the main subject' — this video matches precisely. Specific topics include NVFP4 format, dynamic quantization, mixed-precision layer selection, PTQ vs QAD, and deployment tradeoffs (speed, footprint, concurrency).

secondary.label: Model Foundations & Behavior
secondary.rationale: The panel deeply discusses model intrinsic properties: uneven layer importance (first/last layers critical, middle disposable), weight saturation after 30T training tokens, super weights causing 20% degradation when quantized, and how new hybrid architectures (linear attention, sliding window, MLA) affect model behavior under quantization. These are fundamental model-behavior findings rather than serving concerns.

secondary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
secondary.rationale: The panel extensively discusses evaluation methodology for quantized models: KL divergence between BF16 and quantized logits as the preferred signal over accuracy benchmarks, benchmark limitations (only verifiable tasks, hackable arenas), gradient-based sensitivity analysis with knapsack solving for layer selection, and the absence of a comprehensive resource for evaluating available quants. The paper 'Accuracy is not all you need' is referenced.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: The panel features and discusses major developer-facing tools used for model compression: NVIDIA Model Optimizer, Unsloth quantization, Hugging Face model hub, Ollama runtime, and bitsandbytes. The discussion centers on how builders use these tools to compress and serve models.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: Model compression and quantization techniques discussed are cross-domain, applicable to any LLM deployment from edge devices to cloud infrastructure. The techniques are model-agnostic and not tied to any specific application vertical.

summary: A panel discussion at NVIDIA features representatives from Unsloth (Daniel Han), Hugging Face (Merve Noyan), Ollama (Parth Sareen), and NVIDIA Model Optimizer (Asma Beevi), moderated by Chris Alexiuk. The panel covers model compression and quantization from theoretical foundations, engineering practices, evaluation methodology, and future directions. The anchor example is GLM 5.2's 86% reduction from 1.5TB to 250GB via dynamic quantization with mixed-precision layer selection, recovering 76% of accuracy. Key technical discussions include: why layer importance is highly uneven (first and last layers critical, middle nearly disposable), incomplete weight saturation even after 30 trillion training tokens, super weights causing 20% degradation when quantized, NVFP4 microscaling (16 elements sharing one FP8 scale factor), the PTQ vs QAD threshold at ~20B parameters, and how new hybrid architectures with linear attention layers break quantization heuristics by appearing fine on standard benchmarks but producing gibberish on long-context tasks. The panel debates whether compression matters beyond edge devices—concluding it does, as bigger models quantized down outperform smaller models at native precision at equal disk footprint. Business value extends to concurrency, cost reduction, and in-house deployment. Evaluation methodology is a recurring theme: NVIDIA targets under 1% accuracy degradation using gradient-based sensitivity analysis with a knapsack solver, while Daniel recommends KL divergence between BF16 and quantized logits as the preferred signal over accuracy benchmarks, referencing the paper 'Accuracy is Not All You Need.' Future directions include KV cache compression, dynamic activation sparsity in NVIDIA's Rubin architecture, near-optimal weight quantization at 1-3 bits, and compounding optimization opportunities across heterogeneous attention architectures (MLA, sparse attention, indexed attention). The panel envisions fully democratized intelligence with frontier models running locally on personal devices.
whyItMatters: The software engineering practices (PTQ, QAD, mixed-precision layer selection, NVFP4 microscaling) are directly motivated by AI model properties discovered through research (uneven layer importance, incomplete weight saturation, super weights, linear attention quantization failure). The engineering decisions—whether PTQ suffices or QAD is needed, which layers to quantize at which precision, which format to use—depend entirely on understanding model internals. The evaluation methodology (KL divergence vs accuracy benchmarks) bridges the gap between engineering output and model quality verification, ensuring compressed models behave like their full-precision counterparts. Together, these concepts form a complete pipeline: understanding model structure drives compression strategy, which is implemented through engineering tools (Unsloth, NVIDIA Model Optimizer, bitsandbytes), validated through principled evaluation (KL divergence), and deployed with awareness of architectural constraints (linear attention, hybrid architectures) and future optimization opportunities (KV cache compression, Rubin activation sparsity). The panel format is essential because it shows how these concepts interconnect across organizational boundaries—NVIDIA builds the hardware format, Unsloth implements the dynamic quantization algorithm, Hugging Face distributes the results, and Ollama deploys locally—each depending on shared understanding of the same model properties.
temporalContext: The video was published on 2026-08-07 and recorded in a post-GLM 5.2 era where Unsloth had already demonstrated dynamic quantization of GLM 5.2 from 1.5TB to 250GB. The discussion references NVIDIA's Blackwell GPU architecture as current production hardware and Rubin as the upcoming next-generation architecture with dynamic activation sparsity. Key referenced research: the Super Weight paper was published November 2024 (Apple/Notre Dame), 'Accuracy is Not All You Need' was published July 2024 and accepted at NeurIPS 2024 (Microsoft Research), and the NVFP4 blog was published June 2025 (NVIDIA). The panel reflects state-of-the-art thinking on model compression as of mid-2026, at a moment when weight quantization is approaching theoretical limits and the field is pivoting toward KV cache compression, activation sparsity, and architectural co-design. The open-source quantization ecosystem (Unsloth 74.5k stars, Ollama 179.3k stars, bitsandbytes 8.4k stars) is mature and actively maintained.

concepts.name: Uneven Layer Importance
concepts.explanation: First and last transformer layers are critical to model performance while middle layers are nearly disposable. This non-uniform importance distribution is what enables aggressive compression—most layers can be quantized to very low precision without significant degradation.
concepts.importance: This is the foundational model property that makes all compression techniques viable. Without uneven layer importance, the 86% reduction in GLM 5.2 would be impossible.

concepts.name: Incomplete Weight Saturation
concepts.explanation: Models trained on 30 trillion tokens still do not saturate all parameters, leaving approximately 86% of weights near zero and removable. This explains why compression works far beyond linear expectation.
concepts.importance: Provides the theoretical justification for why massive models can be compressed so aggressively—training does not make all weights meaningful, leaving large removable redundancy.

concepts.name: Super Weights
concepts.explanation: Specific individual parameters whose quantization causes disproportionate model degradation. The Super Weight paper (Apple/Notre Dame) confirms that pruning a single super weight increases perplexity by 3 orders of magnitude and drops zero-shot accuracy from ~70% to ~35%. Super weights are found in mlp.down_proj in early layers.
concepts.importance: Super weights represent the extreme case of uneven parameter importance. Identifying and preserving them during quantization is essential—missing even one can catastrophically degrade model quality.

concepts.name: Linear Attention Quantization Failure
concepts.explanation: Linear attention layers in new hybrid architectures cannot be quantized. They appear to function correctly on standard benchmarks but produce gibberish when evaluated on long-context tasks. This breaks old quantization heuristics that assumed all attention layers behave similarly under compression.
concepts.importance: This is a critical failure mode that practitioners must watch for as model architectures diversify. It shows that quantization heuristics from the Llama era do not transfer to modern hybrid architectures.

concepts.name: KL Divergence as Evaluation Signal
concepts.explanation: KL divergence between BF16 (full precision) and quantized model output logits is the preferred evaluation metric over accuracy benchmarks. The goal is to make the distance zero while shrinking model size. The paper 'Accuracy is Not All You Need' (Microsoft Research, NeurIPS 2024) shows accuracy alone is insufficient—flips can be 5-13% even when accuracy is within 1%.
concepts.importance: This reframes how quantized models should be evaluated, moving away from gaming-prone accuracy benchmarks toward a principled information-theoretic distance measure that captures behavioral fidelity.

concepts.name: Near-Optimal Weight Quantization Limits
concepts.explanation: Weight quantization is approaching near-optimal compression at 1-3 bits per parameter. Future compression gains will come from other sources: KV cache compression, dynamic activation sparsity, and heterogeneous architecture optimization rather than further weight bit-width reduction.
concepts.importance: Signals a paradigm shift in the compression field: the easy wins from weight quantization are nearly exhausted, and researchers must look to activation, KV cache, and architectural co-design for future gains.

concepts.name: Dynamic Activation Sparsity in Rubin
concepts.explanation: NVIDIA's upcoming Rubin architecture introduces dynamic activation sparsity, which can improve attention computation by dynamically sparsifying activations during inference. This represents a hardware-level compression opportunity beyond weight quantization.
concepts.importance: Represents the next frontier of compression at the hardware level, where silicon-level features enable new classes of efficiency gains that software-only approaches cannot achieve.

concepts.name: Heterogeneous Attention Architecture Optimization
concepts.explanation: Modern models use increasingly complex hybrid attention mechanisms—multi-head latent attention (MLA from DeepSeek), sparse attention, indexed attention, sliding window attention—each with different quantization properties. This architectural diversity creates compounding optimization opportunities but also complicates quantization heuristics.
concepts.importance: Architectural diversification is both the greatest challenge and greatest opportunity for future compression. Each new attention type requires its own quantization strategy, but the combination creates optimization space unavailable in uniform architectures.

concepts.name: NVFP4 Microscaling Format
concepts.explanation: A 4-bit float (E2M1: 1 sign, 2 exponent, 1 mantissa) format where every 16 elements share one FP8 (E4M3) scale factor, plus a second-level FP32 per-tensor scale. Originally based on microscaling concepts from bitsandbytes, developed by NVIDIA for Blackwell GPUs. Achieves 3.5x memory reduction vs FP16 with under 1% accuracy degradation.
concepts.importance: NVFP4 is the production quantization format enabling 4-bit inference on NVIDIA Blackwell hardware, directly driving the compression results discussed in the panel. It represents the state-of-the-art in deployment-ready low-precision formats as of 2026.

concepts.name: Post-Training Quantization (PTQ)
concepts.explanation: Applying quantization to an already-trained model without additional training. Works out of the box for models above ~20B parameters, producing condensed checkpoints on Blackwell nodes in hours. Below 20B, quantization-aware distillation is required to recover accuracy.
concepts.importance: PTQ is the dominant production quantization pathway for large models. The 20B threshold is a critical engineering decision point that determines whether a model can be quantized cheaply or requires expensive distillation pipelines.

concepts.name: Quantization-Aware Distillation (QAD)
concepts.explanation: Training a student model to recover accuracy lost during quantization for models below ~20B parameters. Increasingly painful with reasoning models using multi-stage RL training and multi-teacher distillation. Using wrong training data in QAD breaks models rather than helping.
concepts.importance: QAD is the required pathway for small model quantization, and its difficulty with reasoning models represents a major engineering bottleneck for the open-source community quantizing smaller checkpoints.

concepts.name: Combinatorial Layer Selection
concepts.explanation: Selecting which transformer layers to quantize at which precision is a combinatorial optimization problem. Solved using gradient-based sensitivity analysis with a linear programming or knapsack solver to maximize compression while preserving accuracy. First and last layers are kept at high precision; middle layers can be aggressively quantized.
concepts.importance: This is the core algorithmic technique enabling architecture-aware compression. Without intelligent layer selection, random compression makes models 100% dumber rather than 86% smaller, making this the essential trick behind dynamic quantization.

concepts.name: Mixed-Precision Dynamic Quantization
concepts.explanation: Engineering practice of assigning different bit widths to different layers based on sensitivity analysis rather than uniform quantization. GLM 5.2 was compressed with some layers at 16-bit, most at 1-2 bit, and important layers preserved, recovering 76% of accuracy for an 86% size reduction.
concepts.importance: This is the actual technique that produced the panel's anchor example (GLM 5.2: 1.5TB to 250GB). It demonstrates that non-uniform compression vastly outperforms uniform approaches, validating the entire architecture-aware quantization paradigm.

sections.title: Welcome and Panel Introductions
sections.summary: Chris Alexiuk (NVIDIA) introduces the panel. Panelists introduce themselves: Daniel Han (Unsloth), Asma Beevi (NVIDIA Model Optimizer), Merve Noyan (Hugging Face), Parth Sareen (Ollama).

sections.title: Definitions of Compression
sections.summary: Each panelist defines compression. Parth: making giant models viable. Merve: shrinking without losing information, no free lunch. Asma: same cost, more intelligence (FP32 to FP4 = 8x). The panel agrees compression democratizes AI for edge devices.

sections.title: GLM 5.2 Example — 86% Smaller
sections.summary: Daniel Han presents GLM 5.2 going from 1.5TB to 250GB via dynamic quantization. Some layers quantized to higher precision, most at 1-2 bit, important layers at 16 bit, recovering 76% of accuracy. The key is quantizing the correct layers.

sections.title: Origin Stories — Getting the Compression Bug
sections.summary: Daniel's moment: DeepSeek R1, 1.58-bit quant worked randomly and well. Asma: pruning CV models 3 years ago, then NVFP4 research at NVIDIA. Merve: QLoRA on Colab T4, then llama.cpp and Qwen 3.6 quants for agent tasks. Parth: running Llama 3 locally as a broke student in 2023.

sections.title: Verification — Why 86% Smaller Isn't 86% Dumber
sections.summary: Chris asks how to verify a compressed model isn't garbage. Daniel begins explaining that random compression makes models 100% dumber, so leveraging the language model architecture is the essential trick.

sections.title: Layer Importance, Super Weights, and Combinatorial Selection
sections.summary: Daniel explains that first and last layers are critical while middle layers are nearly disposable. Models trained on 30 trillion tokens don't saturate all parameters, leaving ~86% of weights near zero. Selecting which layers to quantize is a combinatorial optimization problem. The super weights paper shows quantizing one specific number degrades the model by 20%.

sections.title: Evaluating Quantized Checkpoints and NVFP4
sections.summary: Asma explains NVIDIA targets under 1% accuracy degradation on AA benchmarks using gradient-based sensitivity analysis with a linear programming solver. Linear attention projection layers (KV, QK, V) are kept at FP4 while others go to FP8 or BF16. Daniel explains NVFP4: 4-bit float with microscaling where every 16 elements share one FP8 scale, originally invented by bitsandbytes.

sections.title: Compression Beyond the Toaster — Business Value
sections.summary: Parth emphasizes benchmarks are insufficient; real validation requires running the model in an actual harness. Merve notes businesses cut millions in costs via quantization and distillation, and that many jobs don't require SOTA-level intelligence. Compression enables increased concurrency and in-house deployment.

sections.title: Why Compress Big Models Instead of Using Small Ones
sections.summary: Daniel cites research showing a 120B model at 4-bit outperforms a 35B model at 16-bit with equal disk footprint. Bigger models compressed down are generally more useful. He notes speed tradeoffs: compressed big models yield 5-10 tokens/sec versus 200 tokens/sec for small models. Model routing can leverage large models for planning and small models for execution.

sections.title: Open Source Community and Personal Models
sections.summary: Parth discusses compression enabling personal language models, noting other formats like Q8_0 and MXFP4 (for GPT-oss). He highlights the open source ecosystem (bitsandbytes, Unsloth, Hugging Face) as the stack holding quantization together. Merve praises Unsloth's quantization pipelines as the best available. She recounts training small VLMs (500M ran on iPhone, 256M was not good enough) and how the Qwen 3.6 community preferred one midsized checkpoint for quantization rather than requesting smaller models, validating quantization's central role.

sections.title: How Hard NVFP4 Is to Produce
sections.summary: Asma explains PTQ is relatively easy for large models (20B+), producing condensed checkpoints on Blackwell nodes in hours, but evaluation and matching the model card is where most time goes. Below 20B, quantization-aware distillation (QAD) is required, which is increasingly painful with reasoning models using multi-stage RL training and multiple teacher distillation. QAD with wrong data breaks models rather than helping. She encourages people that PTQ works out of the box above ~30B.

sections.title: The Cursed Era of Model Architectures
sections.summary: Chris describes the shift from uniform llama-era architectures to a 'cursed era' of hybrid attention, linear attention, and sparse variants. Parth notes two challenges: implementing multiple model variations and finding which quantization works best, sometimes leaving small models in higher precision for better UX. Daniel describes moving from dense 'transformer++' to complex hybrids with sliding window, linear attention, varied activations, and changed layer norm epsilons. Linear attention layers specifically cannot be quantized—they look fine until long-context benchmarks reveal gibberish. Daniel welcomes architectural diversity as healthy for open source.

sections.title: Where Compression Goes Next
sections.summary: The panel forecasts compression's future. Merve sees labs increasingly prioritizing compression at launch, with QAT coming from labs themselves alongside community efforts. Asma sees compression enabling privacy-preserving edge deployment on phones, with Llama CPP developments incoming. Daniel forecasts weight quantization approaching near-optimal limits at 1-3 bit, with future gains from KV cache compression, dynamic activation sparsity in NVIDIA's Rubin architecture, and increasingly complex heterogeneous attention architectures (MLA from DeepSeek, sparse attention, indexed attention) creating compounding optimization opportunities. He envisions fully democratized intelligence running locally on personal devices, letting users own and customize their AI.

sections.title: How Do You Know a Quant Is Any Good
sections.summary: An audience member asks about a comprehensive resource for evaluating available quants for a model. No such resource exists. Daniel explains that accuracy benchmarks are complicated by sampling, trial count, and averaging. Instead, he recommends KL divergence (KLD) between BF16 and quantized output logits as the preferred evaluation signal—the goal is to make the distance zero while shrinking the model. He references the paper 'Accuracy is not all you need.'

technologies.label: NVFP4 Microscaling Quantization Format
technologies.summary: NVFP4 is NVIDIA's 4-bit floating-point format (E2M1: 1 sign, 2 exponent, 1 mantissa) using microscaling where every 16 elements share one FP8 (E4M3) scale factor, with a second-level FP32 per-tensor scale. The format was originally based on blockwise quantization concepts from bitsandbytes and was developed by NVIDIA for Blackwell GPUs, achieving 3.5x memory reduction versus FP16 with under 1% accuracy degradation. NVIDIA targets less than 1% accuracy degradation across benchmarks using gradient-based sensitivity analysis with a linear programming solver to select per-layer precision. KV, QK, and V attention projection layers are kept at FP4 while others go to FP8 or BF16. The format is implemented in NVIDIA's Transformer Engine and Model Optimizer with multiple quantization recipes, and the concept's origin is attributed to bitsandbytes by Daniel Han.
technologies.role: Central quantization format discussed throughout the panel; explained in detail by multiple panelists; anchors the discussion of how 4-bit inference works on modern GPU hardware

technologies.label: Mixed-Precision Dynamic Quantization with Combinatorial Layer Selection
technologies.summary: Mixed-precision dynamic quantization assigns different bit widths to different transformer layers based on sensitivity analysis, treating layer selection as a combinatorial optimization problem solved via gradient-based sensitivity analysis with a knapsack or linear programming solver. First and last layers are kept at high precision (16-bit) while middle layers are aggressively quantized (1-2 bit). Models trained on 30 trillion tokens still do not saturate all parameters, leaving approximately 86% of weights near zero and removable. The anchor example is GLM 5.2 compressed from 1.5TB to 250GB (86% reduction) while recovering 76% of accuracy, versus random compression which makes a model 100% dumber. Super weights—specific individual parameters whose quantization causes disproportionate degradation, found in mlp.down_proj in early layers—must be identified and preserved during the selection process.
technologies.role: Core algorithmic technique behind the panel's anchor example (GLM 5.2 1.5TB to 250GB); central explanation for why compression works far beyond linear expectation

technologies.label: Post-Training Quantization and Quantization-Aware Distillation Pipeline
technologies.summary: The engineering pathway for producing quantized models has a critical threshold at approximately 20B parameters. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) applies quantization to already-trained models without additional training and works out of the box for models above 20B, producing condensed checkpoints on Blackwell nodes in hours. Below 20B, Quantization-Aware Distillation (QAD) is required—training a student model to recover accuracy lost during quantization. QAD is increasingly difficult with reasoning models using multi-stage RL training and multi-teacher distillation, and using wrong training data in QAD breaks models rather than helping. New hybrid architectures with linear attention layers further complicate the pipeline since these layers cannot be quantized without breaking long-context performance—they appear fine on standard benchmarks but produce gibberish on long-context tasks. The panel notes that labs are increasingly prioritizing QAT at launch alongside community-driven quantization.
technologies.role: Defines the production engineering pathway for quantization; the 20B parameter threshold is a critical engineering decision point discussed in detail by Asma Beevi with concrete examples of workflow difficulty

technologies.label: KL Divergence Evaluation Methodology for Compressed Models
technologies.primary: KL Divergence (KLD) Evaluation for Quantized Models
technologies.summary: KL divergence between BF16 (full precision) and quantized model output logits is the preferred evaluation metric over accuracy benchmarks for assessing compressed model quality. The goal is to minimize the distance (ideally zero) while shrinking model size. The paper 'Accuracy is Not All You Need' (Microsoft Research, NeurIPS 2024) demonstrates that accuracy alone is insufficient—flips can be 5-13% even when accuracy is within 1%—and that KL divergence and % flips are well-correlated (Spearman 0.981 on MMLU). Daniel Han recommends this as the primary evaluation signal, noting that accuracy benchmarks are complicated by sampling, trial count, and averaging requirements, and that no comprehensive resource exists for evaluating the suite of available quants for a given model. This methodology becomes increasingly critical as weight quantization approaches near-optimal limits at 1-3 bits and future compression shifts to KV cache, activation sparsity, and heterogeneous architecture optimization.
technologies.role: Recommended evaluation methodology in the final Q&A segment; Daniel Han's preferred signal for assessing quantized model quality, presented as the answer to an audience question about evaluating available quants

resources.why: Shows concrete NVFP4 quantization schemes (nvfp4_default, nvfp4_weight_only, kv_nvfp4_cast) and their configuration, confirming the panel discussion of layer-level precision selection and PTQ working out of the box for large models (evidence_ids 84dfefff, 49d68ee7)

resources.title: About Unsloth
resources.why: Unsloth founded by brothers Daniel Han (co-founder and CEO) and Michael Han (co-founder). YC S24 backed startup founded 2023, headquartered in San Francisco with approximately 16 employees.

resources.title: unslothai/unsloth: Local UI to run and train LLMs and diffusion models
resources.why: Unsloth GitHub repository has 74.5k stars with dual Apache-2.0/AGPL-3.0 license. Provides open-source tools for running, training, and deploying LLMs locally including quantization export to NVFP4 and GGUF formats.

resources.title: Hugging Face — The AI community building the future.
resources.why: Hugging Face is the collaboration platform for the ML community hosting 2M+ models, 500k+ datasets, and 1M+ applications. Builds widely-used open-source libraries including Transformers, Diffusers, and Tokenizers.

resources.title: Ollama — Get up and running with large language models
resources.why: Ollama provides local and cloud LLM deployment with open model weights and open-source code. Supports macOS, Windows, and Linux. Privacy-preserving with offline capability.

resources.title: ollama/ollama: Get up and running with LLMs
resources.why: Ollama open-source repository has 179.3k stars with MIT license. Supports multiple model formats including GGUF via llama.cpp backend. Cross-platform support for macOS, Windows, and Linux.

resources.title: bitsandbytes-foundation/bitsandbytes: Accessible large language models via k-bit quantization for PyTorch
resources.why: bitsandbytes is an MIT-licensed open-source quantization library maintained by bitsandbytes-foundation on GitHub with 8.4k stars. Provides LLM.int8(), QLoRA 4-bit quantization, and 8-bit optimizers. Originated blockwise k-bit quantization concepts. Sponsored by Hugging Face.

resources.title: The Super Weight in Large Language Models
resources.why: Apple ML Research hosts the Super Weight paper, confirming the research was conducted by Apple researchers. Pruning a single super weight can destroy LLM text generation: perplexity increases by 3 orders of magnitude, zero-shot accuracy drops from ~70% to ~35%.

resources.title: Accuracy is Not All You Need
resources.why: Microsoft Research hosts the publication page for 'Accuracy is Not All You Need', confirming the research was conducted by Microsoft Research authors. Proposes KL-Divergence and % flips as evaluation metrics for compressed LLMs.

resources.title: The Super Weight in Large Language Models
resources.why: Confirms that pruning a single super weight destroys LLM text generation (perplexity increases 3 orders of magnitude, zero-shot accuracy drops to guessing from ~70% to ~35%). Super weights are found in mlp.down_proj in early layers. Directly verifies transcript claim (evidence_id e60e63e1). Authors from Apple and University of Notre Dame.

resources.title: Accuracy is Not All You Need
resources.why: Proposes KL-Divergence and % flips as distance metrics for evaluating compressed LLMs, showing accuracy alone is insufficient (flips can be 5-13% even when accuracy is within 1%). KL-Divergence and flips well correlated (Spearman 0.981 on MMLU). Accepted at NeurIPS 2024. Directly verifies transcript claim (evidence_id f4c1a2e3). Authors from Microsoft Research.

resources.title: Accuracy is Not All You Need
resources.why: Paper accepted and published at NeurIPS 2024 conference proceedings, confirming peer-reviewed status of the KL-divergence and flips methodology for evaluating compressed LLMs.
